# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
This report answers the questions the earlier documents left open, and it does so mostly well. It uses log-measured hours, a registered mediation test and a controlled two-year follow-up. Its central result is credible: a per-hour gain of about 8.5–10% that has faded somewhat but not disappeared. The main problems are that the summary overstates the decline and the strength of the mediation result, and that the report misses a contamination of its own control group.

## The numbers mostly check out

- **Per-hour figures.** 0.966/0.88 = 1.098, so +9.8% on timesheets. 0.966/0.89 = 1.085, so +8.5% on logs.
- **Intervals.** The intervals are centred on these estimates in log terms. For example, 4.6–15.2 has a log midpoint of 0.093, which is +9.8%.
- **Halden.** 34.9/40.3 = 0.866, a fall of 13.4%, and 0.968/0.866 = 1.118, a gain of 11.8%.
- **Meetings.** Treated offices at 3.9 hours and control offices at 7.0 match the month-six figures in the nine-month report (3.8 vs 7.1).
- **Counter arm.** Waiting times worsened from 6.9 minutes at month 9 to 7.3 in months 10–12.

Three things don't quite fit:

**1. The summary compares different measures.**
"Fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months" compares a timesheet figure with a log figure. The like-for-like comparison is **12.5% → 9.8%**, a fall of about 22%, not 32%. Section 3 gets this right; the summary doesn't. No test of whether the decline is statistically significant is reported either, and the two intervals overlap heavily.

**2. It's unclear what the system logs measure.**
- **The report's description.** It says logs record "time staff are working on cases".
- **What that would imply.** Recurring meetings fell by about 3.3 hours relative to control, while timesheet hours fell about 4.5 hours. Case-work time would then have fallen only about 1.2 hours, roughly 4%.
- **What the report shows instead.** Log hours fell 11%, almost as much as timesheet hours.
- **The likely explanation.** Logs probably include time logged in during meetings or idle time, so they measure total time more than case work.
- **What to ask.** The authors should say what "active log-in time" includes. They should also say whether log data existed for the baseline period, since a difference-in-differences estimate needs it and the nine-month report had none.

**3. The cost figure needs explaining.**
- **The arithmetic.** If 12% more staff restores contacts handled (1.12 × 0.886 ≈ 0.99), the *staff* cost per contact rises about 13%, not 9%.
- **A possible reason.** The 9% would fit if staff costs are about 70% of total cost per contact.
- **What to ask.** The report should state this assumption.

## What it does well

- **It applies the critics' standards.** The follow-up uses record-based output, log hours, randomisation and two years of follow-up. This addresses the re-analysis on its own terms.
- **It registered the mediation test first.** The test was filed at month 11, before the 24-month data existed, with named mediators and a single outcome.
- **It reports results against its own interest.** The gain declined, output per FTE drifted to −3.4%, and the counter arm failed badly enough to be ended.
- **It treats the Halden subset honestly.** It calls the subset "survivors twice over" and an upper bound.
- **It checks the meta-analysis claim properly.** It examined the four long-follow-up studies in the meta-analysis. All four were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours, which supports the doubts I raised about the meta-analysis's "no sign of decay".
- **It frames the meeting-audit observation cautiously.** It also raises the open question of whether cutting hours is what makes reorganisation happen.

## Problems

**1. The control group was contaminated, and the report doesn't say so.**
- **What happened.** Two of the seven control offices carried out a meeting audit at month 15 and raised output per hour by about 4%.
- **Why it matters.** This improves the control group, which reduces the treatment-vs-control gap at 24 months. Roughly, 2/7 × 4% is about 1 percentage point over part of the period.
- **The consequence.** Part of the apparent decline from 12.5% to 9.8% may come from controls getting better, not from treated offices fading. The meetings mediation estimate is also affected.
- **A likely cause.** The audits probably weren't independent of the trial. They followed the publication of the nine-month report, which highlighted meetings.
- **How the report presents it.** It calls this "an unplanned observation" about whether reorganisation alone works, but doesn't discuss what it means for its own estimates. It should report results with and without those two offices.

**2. "Confirms" overstates the mediation result.**
- **The assumptions are untested.** Mediation in a trial requires that nothing unmeasured affects both the mediators and the outcome. The limitations section admits this cannot be guaranteed. A registered test makes the finding confirmatory rather than exploratory, but it doesn't make it causal.
- **The sample is still small.** Using more office-months doesn't add independent units; there are still 7 + 7 offices. An interval of 28–66% looks tight for 14 clusters, and the inference method is still not stated.
- **It isn't fully a replication.** The 24-month data include the months that produced the exploratory hypothesis, so the test isn't entirely on new data.
- **The shares may not add up.** Fewer meetings may themselves reduce fatigue. If so, the 47% and 18% overlap, and the 35% "unexplained" depends on how the model handles that.
- **A related question.** The nine-month report mentioned no fatigue measure. When was the fatigue scale first given? If only after month 11, the 0.34 SD "improvement" has no baseline.

**3. Simple accounting suggests meetings might explain more than 47%.**
- **The calculation.** Using timesheet hours, non-meeting time was about 30.5/37.9 = 80% of hours at baseline and about 29.5/33.4 = 88% at 24 months. That is a rise of about 10%, roughly the whole 9.8% gain.
- **What that implies.** If removed meeting time produced no output, output per hour of actual case work barely changed.
- **Why the mediation model may differ.** Either some cancelled meetings had value, or measurement error in the calendar data is pulling the mediation estimate down.
- **The caveat.** This is rough. But it suggests 47% may be a lower bound, which makes the cheaper option of cutting meetings without cutting hours more relevant.

**4. The Halden framing is too neat.**
- **The reversions aren't all coverage-bound.** The summary says all three had "client-facing or coverage obligations". One was a marketing agency citing client deadlines, which the meta-analysis's coding would class as *discretionary*. So discretionary work can fail too.
- **Missing details.** Only 14 of 23 organisations responded, and the report doesn't say whether all 11 continuing organisations have time tracking. The baseline of 40.3 hours is the 27-organisation figure from the re-analysis, not necessarily this subset's own.

**5. Small-cluster inference is still not addressed.**
With 7 offices per arm, the statement that the interval "excludes zero by a clear margin" depends on how the standard errors were computed. A small-sample correction may widen the 3.4–13.8 interval. This was an issue in the nine-month report and is still unreported.

**6. The authors have a stake in the conclusions.**
- **The authors.** They are the original Varden team, who proposed the meetings hypothesis, plus the Halden lead author.
- **Section 5.** It rebuts the critics of both.
- **How much this matters.** It doesn't invalidate the findings, and the registered design limits how much it can matter. Readers should still notice that the authors are marking their own critics' work. Independent replication of the mediation result would carry more weight.

## Where things now stand

| Question | Before this report | Now |
|---|---|---|
| Per-hour gain, discretionary work | About 8–10% (meta-analysis, short-term) | About 8.5–10% at 24 months in the best study |
| Does it decay? | Unknown | Some decline from 9 to 24 months, possibly overstated by control contamination; not to zero |
| Meta-analysis "no decay" claim | Weak | Undermined, since its four long studies were all uncontrolled with scheduled hours |
| "Entirely an artifact" | Not supported | Contradicted by a study meeting the critics' own standards |
| Mechanism | Unknown | Meetings are the leading candidate (registered, about half or more); fatigue is secondary; untested causal assumptions remain |
| Coverage-bound work | Output per worker −9 to −11% | Unsustainable without about 12% more staff; the county ended the arm |
| Can the gain be had without cutting hours? | Not asked | Plausibly in part (two control offices), but untested; this needs a meetings-only arm |
| Output per employee, discretionary work | About −2 to −3% | About −3.4%, interval includes zero; the cut is mostly but not fully paid for |

**Bottom line.** Across all five documents, the evidence supports a real but modest gain in output per hour, about a tenth, in work not tied to staff presence. That gain persists over two years, and much of it seems to come from removing low-value meeting time rather than from rest. Output per employee ends slightly below where it started. In coverage-bound work, the change costs service or staff.

The most useful next study would randomise three arms: reduced hours, meetings reorganisation at full hours, and control. That would show whether the hours cut is the cause of the gain or mainly what prompts the reorganisation. In the meantime, the 24-month estimates should be reported with and without the two control offices that ran meeting audits.
